sources.news_title: ‘Urgent requirements’ for US military funding cited by GOP as Hegseth estimates war cost
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate committee in charge of funding the government spent hours in a hearing room Tuesday, trying to parse out just how much extra spending lawmakers should provide for the military amid the ongoing war in Iran.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators the bombing of Iran has cost $37.5 billion. He said that while the department has about $75 billion in unobligated funds from Republicans’ “big, beautiful” law, that money wasn’t intended to cover the costs of the war.
Republicans and Democrats on the Appropriations Committee also heard from three of their colleagues about the need for natural disaster recovery funding and the secretary of Agriculture about her request for emergency aid for farmers.
Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, summed up the multitude of proposals for additional money by saying the “country has many urgent funding needs.”
Collins said that while there were vastly different views among senators on the panel about the war, “the fact remains that there are must-pay bills and urgent requirements facing the department that affect the ability of our troops to be well trained and more broadly of the U.S. military to deter and defend against potential aggressors worldwide.”
Washington Democratic Sen. Patty Murray, ranking member on the committee, said at the beginning of the three-and-a-half hour hearing the United States “is no safer or better off than before the war.”
“In fact, we are considerably less safe. Our stockpiles have been depleted and it will take years of production to fully replenish them no matter how much money is thrown at this problem,” Murray said.
By the end of the hearing, she indicated Democrats may not support any emergency funding for the Defense Department related to the Iran war.
“Unfortunately, this hearing has done exceptionally little to justify the president’s request or to instill confidence that this administration has an exit plan or a strategy to end the war,” Murray said. “This war has cost us a lot. The last thing we should be doing is rubber stamping another $70 billion to help Trump keep it going.”
Hegseth warns of ‘critical shortfalls’
Hegseth said that without extra money from Congress, the department would “face critical shortfalls that threaten” its ability to “pay our service members, rapidly replenish equipment and munitions, and sustain vital operations without disruption.”
Hegseth repeatedly defended the Iran war during the hearing, pressing back on criticism from several Democrats that it was similar to earlier wars in the Middle East.
“President Trump said we’re not fighting stupid wars like that again and he hasn’t,” Hegseth said. “That’s why we haven’t been trying to remake Iranian society, but simply in the realist America First way, ensure they never have a path to a nuclear bomb, full stop.”
He declined to go into detail in a non-classified setting about the aid China and Russia has provided to Iran, but did say those two countries are “enabling some of the things Iran is doing.”
Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. John D. Caine said he’d prefer not discuss the intelligence about those two countries.
“I’d rather not opine on the specifics because that would divulge what we know. And I never want the adversary to know what I know. I just want to know it,” he said.
Caine also declined to go into any level of detail about whether the administration has contemplated sending ground troops into Iran.
“I think it’d be unhelpful for me to opine on hypothetical situations on whatever decisions the president may or may not take in the future,” Caine said.
Trump's request to Congress
Congress approved $838.7 billion for the Defense Department in February as part of the annual government funding process. A few weeks later, President Donald Trump began bombing Iran, starting a war that has led to the deaths of 17 U.S. service members — including three in the last few days — and injured more than 445.
The administration sent a supplemental spending request to Congress in late June, asking lawmakers to provide $87.6 billion in emergency funding. It proposed an additional:
- $67.15 billion for the Defense Department
- $11.1 billion for the Agriculture Department to provide aid to farmers
- $3.36 billion for the State Department for diplomatic, security and global health programs
- $2.03 billion for the U.S. Coast Guard
- $1 billion for the Transportation Department to “to assist in the final design and construction of a modernized Penn Station in New York City”
- $1 billion for the Labor Department to “increase the benefit levels for participants of certain pension plans that were sponsored by Delphi Corporation and terminated as a result of General Motors’ bankruptcy in 2009″
- $767.5 million for the Energy Department
- $600 million for the General Services Administration’s federal buildings fund
- $500 million for the National Park Service to upgrade a seawall and improve the World War II Memorial
- $40.26 million for the FBI for its role in the Iran war and “other classified needs”
- $36.18 million for the Treasury Department’s office of terrorism and financial intelligence
- $13.1 million for the Homeland Security Department’s operations and support account that was part of a “classified request.”
House Republicans want to use the complex budget reconciliation process to provide up to $60 billion for the Defense Department and $12 billion for farm aid.
But that effort hasn’t yet garnered the support from Senate Republicans needed to advance. GOP lawmakers used the same process last year to bolster defense funding by about $150 billion in the “big, beautiful” law.
That means the most likely path to provide extra money for the war and farmers will be a bipartisan supplemental spending bill, likely written by the Appropriations Committees.
With the House set to leave Thursday for its August recess and the Senate planning to leave for its break on Aug. 6, the earliest any additional funding would become law is September.
Farm aid
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the administration’s request for emergency funding would help farmers, including those who have experienced extreme weather events.
Collins, however, questioned the administration’s decision to limit its request for supplemental funding to agriculture losses that took place during the last year.
“Many of our producers are struggling amid a combination of market volatility and disaster conditions last year, which included excessive rainfall in the spring, followed by a severe drought. They need relief. Yet the administration’s supplemental request does not include funding to address these recovery needs,” Collins said. “It does have $1.1 billion to help Florida agricultural producers rebound from a severe freeze this past winter. But nothing for prior disasters in other states.”
Rollins said she would be in full support of Congress providing more funding than requested for farmers affected by severe weather events.
Oregon Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley asked Rollins to ensure the Office of Management and Budget sends lawmakers a specific request to address ongoing costs related to wildfires.
“Senators are asking for a number from OMB in order to go forward,” he said. “And when we’re looking at the fires right now, my home state is in the epicenter of the highest risk in the country.”
Rollins said she would “absolutely” get that number to lawmakers, adding it “is a paramount importance, especially in the middle of fire season right now.”

sources.news_title: Hegseth puts Iran war cost at $37.5B, seeks $67B more
sources.text:
Hegseth puts Iran war cost at $37.5B, seeks $67B more
The additional funding was described as an “urgent, necessary” stopgap
What happened
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate committee on Tuesday that President Donald Trump’s Iran war had cost an estimated $37.5 billion so far, and that the $67 billion in supplemental war funding he was requesting is an “urgent, necessary” stopgap as Congress debates Trump’s $1.5 trillion annual Pentagon budget request. Hegseth faced “fiery questions” during the “combative Senate Appropriations Committee hearing,” The Associated Press said. And the scrutiny was “bipartisan,” The Washington Post said, as “frustrated lawmakers” pressed him to “explain the Trump administration’s strategy for the war” amid “renewed hostilities.”
Who said what
Hegseth’s appearance “represented an attempt by the administration to sell the unpopular conflict as a necessary expense,” Politico said. But Senate Democrats “questioned both the success of the war so far and the need for more military money, citing $75 billion in unused funds” from last year’s huge GOP-only spending package. “The problem is not a lack of money, but poor planning,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) told Hegseth. “This war is now spiraling out of control again,” and Trump is “asking for $70 billion more — and for us to just trust him it’ll all work out fine.”
What next?
The House plans to quit Washington on Thursday “for a month-long recess,” the Post said, “leaving any deal on military funding weeks away at the earliest.”

sources.news_title: 'Was that an accurate statement?': Ossoff quotes Hegseth's own words on Iran back to him. Then asks him a simple yes-or-no question
sources.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Monday, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia questioned him repeatedly about past statements on the war with Iran. Hegseth testified as the Trump administration seeks an additional $70 billion for the war effort, according to the hearing.
During the hearing, Hegseth said the war has cost $37.5 billion so far. President Donald Trump, who started the conflict at the end of February, has not signaled an end to the war, according to the report.
According to The Daily Beast, Ossoff used several of Hegseth’s earlier comments about the war against him during the exchange, asking the secretary directly whether those statements had been accurate.
Ossoff presses Hegseth on ‘combat ineffective’ claim
Ossoff noted that on day 14 of the conflict, nearly five months before the hearing, Hegseth had said Iran’s military had been “destroyed” and “made combat ineffective.” Ossoff then asked Hegseth directly, “Was that an accurate statement?”
In response, Hegseth said Iran no longer had a navy, saying it was “completely sunk.” He also said missiles were “buried underneath a lot of their underground facilities” and said Iran’s “defense industrial base has been almost completely destroyed.”
Hegseth then said, “So, as far as a military assessment of Iran’s capabilities, it didn’t mean by any stretch of the imagination absolute zero – ” before Ossoff cut him off. Ossoff repeated his question, asking again whether Hegseth’s day-14 statement had been accurate, “yes or no.” Hegseth did not give a direct yes-or-no answer and instead began discussing “Iran’s ability to challenge the United States of America.”
Ossoff told Hegseth that was not what he had asked and repeated the question a third time using Hegseth’s own words. Hegseth again did not answer directly, instead saying, “What the American military has done to the Iranian military – ” before Ossoff asked, “Will you answer the question?” Hegseth then called the outcome an “historic military defeat” for Iran, according to the exchange. Ossoff moved on without receiving a direct response, the report noted.
Ossoff then referenced comments Hegseth made three weeks after the “combat ineffective” statement, in which Hegseth reportedly called the military campaign, named Operation Epic Fury, “a historic and overwhelming victory.” Hegseth had also said Iran’s military had been made “combat ineffective for years to come” and that the U.S. had “achieved every single objective,” according to Ossoff’s recounting of the remarks.
Asked whether those statements had been accurate, Hegseth said, “It certainly was, on behalf of the men and women in uniform, a historic military victory over Iran.”
When Ossoff asked again whether Iran’s military had been rendered “combat ineffective for years to come,” Hegseth said Iran’s “160 naval vessels in their bluewater Navy” were gone, and claimed Iran’s air force was “completely combat ineffective” and that the country lacked a defense industrial base.
As Ossoff pressed him to answer directly, Hegseth raised his voice and said, “So describe for me a country that doesn’t have an air force, a navy or a defense industrial base, and I will describe for you a country that doesn’t have an effective military.”
Ossoff continued his questions as Hegseth reportedly spoke over him at points. Hegseth’s handling of the exchange comes amid separate reports that half of Republican staffers say he is hurting Trump’s foreign agenda.
Asked again whether Iran’s military had remained “combat ineffective” for four months, Hegseth said Iran’s capabilities had been “set back not just years but likely decades.” He then said, “It doesn’t mean it doesn’t have capabilities,” according to the exchange.
When Ossoff asked whether the administration had “achieved every single objective,” Hegseth said the main objective was preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, saying Iran’s “main sites were obliterated.” He added that if Iran does not give up its nuclear program “at the table, there are other ways we can take them away.”
Ossoff also raised earlier statements from Hegseth about destroying Iran’s missile threat, noting Hegseth had said on day three of the conflict that one objective was to “destroy the missile threat,” and on day five had said the goal was to “obliterate Iran’s missiles and drones.” Ossoff asked whether those objectives had been achieved.
Hegseth said, “No one ever stated that every single missile was gone,” and said “combat-ineffective means they’re not able to dig them out of their UGFs and shoot at us.” He added that Iran, which he described as “the world’s largest state sponsor of terrorism,” still holds underground facilities with missiles. Hegseth’s credibility on military communications has also faced scrutiny after a Pentagon watchdog investigated his handling of a secret war chat.
Ossoff also asked whether Hegseth’s March 8 prediction of “Iranian surrender” remained accurate. Hegseth did not directly address the prediction and instead said, “Ultimately Iran will never have a nuclear weapon to threaten the United States of America,” calling that the continuing objective.
Other senators also questioned Hegseth during the hearing. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand criticized the administration’s funding request, saying, “The words you have used in the past don’t add up,” while raising concerns about spending on the war compared with domestic health care and food assistance, according to the hearing.
Sen. Jack Reed also questioned Hegseth about the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which he said has driven up prices. Hegseth said the administration had anticipated the possibility of the Strait closing, then referenced past incidents under the Biden administration.
Reed responded, “We are talking a war you started,” and said Hegseth’s comparison to the Biden administration was “a very, very obvious excuse of what I think is probably, as you describe it so often, gross negligence.”
The hearing was also interrupted by protesters, who were removed from the room by Capitol Police/

sources.news_title: Hegseth reveals how much the Iran war has cost so far
sources.text:
Hegseth reveals how much the Iran war has cost so far
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provided a new estimate for the cost of war against Iran this week as Republicans prepare another $95 billion for the military and Democrats say the five-month conflict is "spiraling out of control."
Hegseth gave an update during a fiery Senate Appropriations Committee hearing Tuesday.
How much has the Iran war cost so far?
By the numbers:
Hegseth said the Iran war has cost an estimated $37.5 billion so far. He’s asking Congress for an additional $95 billion in supplemental funding, along with the White House’s request for a $1.5 trillion defense budget.
RELATED: Name released of soldier missing after Iran attack on air base and presumed dead
The proposed budget package includes $60 billion and $12 billion for other national security needs, along with $10 billion for farm aid and $10 billion for voting law changes.
What they're saying:
In a statement released before the hearing, the White House urged support of the budget resolution, "without modification — immediately."
"Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls," Hegseth testified.
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, DC. Members of the Trump administration appeared before the committee
The other side:
Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the committee, called it "another forever war."
"This war is now spiraling out of control again," Murray said.
President Donald Trump has said repeatedly that "a deal is near, and the war will be over soon," she said. "But now, he’s asking for $70 billion more — and for us to just trust him it’ll all work out fine."
Hegseth erupted after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan said the administration’s war strategy has been a complete "failure."
"Shame on you and others who call this a quagmire and a failure," Hegseth said.
"You, sir, are the failure," Peters snapped back.
"You don’t have a strategy," Peters said. "You don’t have a long-term plan to actually win this war."
Most Americans disapprove of Iran war
Dig deeper:
Most Americans continue to disapprove of how Trump is handling Iran, according to an AP-NORC poll. A recent poll by Gallup found that only 34% of Americans said they approved of the military action being taken in Iran.
Still, Trump shows no signs of ending the war anytime soon.
What's next:
The GOP is expected to pass the defense budget using the reconciliation process, which allows Republicans to bypass Democrats who object.
The proposal is headed toward a House vote this week, which would start the process by instructing various committees to begin drafting the legislation. House Speaker Mike Johnson can afford only a few defectors from his slim majority, and some conservatives want the funding offset with spending reductions elsewhere.
GOP senators have so far panned the House budget plan, but are waiting to see if Johnson can kickstart the process.

sources.news_title: US Reveals Secret Hormuz Operation as Iran War Cost Hits $37.5B
sources.text:
President Trump warned Wednesday that the U.S. will destroy one Iranian bridge or power plant — including targets in Tehran — every time Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, escalating the standoff as he continues weighing whether to accept a 10-day ceasefire or launch a full-scale campaign with Israel.
WHAT HAPPENED
"From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT," Trump wrote on Truth Social, specifying that targets include those "located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran." The threat follows Trump's previous warnings to strike Iranian civilian infrastructure, including electrical plants and water facilities — threats experts have said could constitute war crimes under international law if carried out.
An unnamed Iranian military source told the state-run Tasnim News Agency that Iran would respond in kind, saying that if the U.S. targets a bridge or power plant, "Iran will, in turn, strike infrastructure and bridges in the region, including energy facilities where the United States has interests." The source said Iran remained determined to control passage through the strait, saying ships would be allowed safe transit only if coordinated with Tehran under Iranian arrangements. CENTCOM said Iran has attacked more than 30 commercial vessels over the past three months, including several after the U.S. and Iran signed a June memorandum of understanding calling for a ceasefire.
The threat came after the U.S. carried out its 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, with CENTCOM saying it hit Iranian military operations centers, drone storage facilities and military logistics infrastructure as it continues trying to clear the Hormuz Strait, the vital oil shipping route that has become Tehran's key source of leverage in the war. Iranian air defenses opened fire over Tehran during the strikes. Iran separately launched a missile at a Jordanian city near Israel's border, and alerts were issued in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. Earlier Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting in Manila that Iran is "not serious" about reaching a deal, saying Tehran had made commitments in last month's memorandum of understanding "and within two weeks violated it." Rubio said the U.S. remains open to negotiating with Iran but warned "there will be consequences" if Tehran continues violating its commitments. Rubio separately credited China for taking what he called a constructive public position supporting freedom of navigation through Hormuz, though he declined to say whether Beijing has provided Iran any material support.
Separately, Trump approved a nuclear agreement that could allow Saudi Arabia to enrich its own uranium for civilian reactors, according to a U.S. official; Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said he would pursue his own nuclear weapons should Iran acquire one. Benchmark Brent crude rose to around $94 a barrel in trading, with gasoline prices climbing again.
President Trump traveled to Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Wednesday to participate in the dignified transfer of four fallen American service members, including Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Fayetteville, North Carolina. "We're going to Dover," Trump told reporters ahead of the trip. "Some of you are going with us, to honor our heroes... we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Iran's Ministry of Health said U.S. strikes have killed 53 people and injured 592 over the past month, including six women and three children among the dead and 39 women and 23 people under 18 among the injured. CENTCOM said it has helped facilitate the transit of roughly 900 commercial vessels and 450 million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz since early May, even as the Joint Maritime Information Center in Bahrain said commercial traffic through the strait fell to a three-week low Tuesday amid the ongoing attacks.
Five oil tankers changed course in the Red Sea on Wednesday after Yemen's Houthi rebels warned ships to avoid Saudi Arabian ports, part of the naval blockade the Iran-aligned group declared this week, opening a new front in the war beyond the Persian Gulf.
WHY IT MATTERS
Trump's new automatic-retaliation policy — a fixed, publicly declared response tied to each Iranian attack rather than a case-by-case decision — removes ambiguity about how Washington will respond to future strikes on shipping, but doing so by name-checking Tehran itself marks a significant escalation beyond the campaign's earlier focus on ports and shipping infrastructure. Iran's vow to strike regional energy infrastructure with U.S. interests in response signals the countries are moving toward a more codified cycle of tit-for-tat escalation rather than negotiating an off-ramp, even as the ceasefire-versus-full-war decision Trump is weighing remains unresolved. The approval of a Saudi nuclear enrichment agreement, arriving amid the standoff over Iran's own nuclear program, could complicate the broader regional nonproliferation picture regardless of how the current conflict resolves. The human toll on both sides — American service members returning in flag-draped cases at Dover, and Iran's own reported casualty figures climbing into the hundreds — underscores that the war's costs are mounting in parallel with its economic disruption, even as both governments continue trading threats over the strait's future. Rising oil prices and falling shipping traffic through Hormuz, despite CENTCOM's efforts to keep commerce moving, suggest the economic strain is deepening even where military efforts have had some success.
WHAT'S NEXT
Whether Iran tests the new bridge-and-power-plant policy with another attack on shipping will determine how quickly the threatened strikes on Tehran-area infrastructure materialize, a step that would mark a significant deepening of the campaign. Trump's decision between the ceasefire proposal and a full-scale campaign with Israel remains outstanding, and continued strikes on both sides make the diplomatic window mediators have sought to preserve increasingly narrow. The Houthi blockade's effect on Red Sea shipping, layered atop the Hormuz disruption, will be watched closely as a second front that could further strain global oil markets. Rising fuel prices heading into the fall will likely sharpen the political stakes of the decision ahead of the November midterms.

sources.news_title: U.S. defense secretary seeks more funding for Iran war despite anti-war sentiment
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, July 22 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday asked for more funding for the U.S. war against Iran at a Senate hearing, as a recent poll found the majority of Americans believe the war is not worth fighting.
Supplemental funding for the war with Iran is "urgent, necessary," Hegseth testified during the Senate Appropriations Committee hearing.
"Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls," said Hegseth, whose opening remarks were interrupted multiple times by protesters, some holding signs that read "No War on Iran."
At the hearing, Hegseth said the U.S. war against Iran has cost 37.5 billion U.S. dollars so far, up from the 29 billion dollars estimated in May.
Hegseth's remarks came as Republican lawmakers sought congressional approval for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed 1.5-trillion-dollar defense budget, even as a growing number of polls showed rising public backlash against the war on Iran.
A recent Washington Post-Ipsos poll found that 68 percent of Americans believe the war is not "worth fighting."
The Washington Post noted that the assessment of this war is worse than in any Post-ABC News poll during the long Iraq War and on par with the worst ratings of the war in Afghanistan, which came in July 2013, when 67 percent said that conflict was not worth fighting.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in June showed that 45 percent of voters said the United States was in a weaker position in the world as a result of the U.S. war against Iran. ■

sources.news_title: Iran war already cost US $37.5 billion yet Pentagon asks for more
sources.text:
The ongoing Iran war has cost the United States an estimated $37.5 billion so far, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth revealed Tuesday, up from a previous estimate of nearly $29 billion in mid-May.
"The estimate we have as of today is $37.5 billion," Hegseth testified during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing at which he defended a request for some $67 billion in supplemental funding for the Pentagon.
Hegseth and General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told Congress the funding request is "urgent" and "necessary" to pay the Pentagon's costs for the Iran war through the end of September.
But Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen challenged that assessment, saying Hegseth still has $75 billion available in unspent funding.
"Why are you asking the American people to absorb the cost of a war they don't support instead of asking for transfer authority for unspent reconciliation funding?"
Hegseth said the unspent money was "otherwise allocated" for President Donald Trump's other priorities, like the "Golden Dome for America and hypersonics and other munitions investments."
The requested funds do not include what it will cost to rebuild U.S. military bases in the Middle East.
Lawmakers voiced frustration as they pressed for details of the Trump administration's strategy to win the war in the Middle East.
Demands for transparency crossed partisan lines, with Republican Sen. John Kennedy saying "we need some hard answers and some straight talk" when he asked what would happen if the U.S. just left the Strait of Hormuz.
Hegseth and Caine did not offer specifics for whether Iran would impose fees for ships seeking passage.

sources.news_title: Iran war has cost US $37.5bn so far, Hegseth says as Pentagon seeks billions more
sources.text:
Iran war has cost US $37.5bn so far, Hegseth says as Pentagon seeks billions more
WASHINGTON — US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has put the latest official price tag on the US-Israel war on Iran at $37.5 billion, an increase of nearly $8 billion since the last estimate in May.
Hegseth confirmed the figure during a hearing before the Senate appropriations committee on Tuesday, in which he and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine were questioned about their request for a $1.5 trillion US defense budget, including nearly $70 billion for the war with Iran.
Hegseth told the committee it was urgent that lawmakers approve another $87 billion in congressional funding for the Pentagon, with $67 billion of that destined for operations in the Middle East.
The hearing was disrupted several times by anti-war protesters and ended in a shouting match between the defense secretary and a senator.
It was Hegseth's first appearance on Capitol Hill since hostilities between the US and Iran restarted last week and comes after three American soldiers were confirmed killed in the region.
The White House asked Congress in April for $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon over the next fiscal year, which would raise American military spending to an all-time high in the modern era.
The defense secretary began Tuesday's testimony by saying, "we live in a dangerous world" and that it required bold and swift action.
After being interrupted by protesters, Hegseth went on to say his funding request came at an urgent time.
"Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls that threaten our ability to also simply pay our service members, rapidly replenish equipment and munitions, and sustain vital operations without disruption," Hegseth said.
Every dollar appropriated, he added, would be used to build the "lethality" of US military forces and "reinforce peace through strength".
Senate Appropriations Committee chairwoman Susan Collins, a Republican, questioned Hegseth over what the impact would be if the budget needs were not met.
Hegseth said current and future training for military members would need to be cut without the funds, as he repeatedly blamed former President Joe Biden's administration for what he said was an underfunded military.
The most senior Democrat on the committee, Patty Murray, pushed back on the funding request, saying it "does not make a lot of sense".
Asked by Democratic Senator Dick Durbin if he had an estimate for how much the war in Iran has cost so far, Hegseth gave the $37.5 billion figure.
Two Democratic sources and a third source familiar with the matter told CBS that they believe the actual cost of the Iran war is much higher. They said the current estimate did not include costs like reconstruction for damaged American bases.
There had been no official government estimate of the US financial cost of the war since 12 May, when a senior Pentagon official put the figure at $29 billion.
The Pentagon previously told lawmakers the war had cost the US some $11.3 billion in the first week.
The Pentagon chief argued that if approved, the funding request would be a "generational investment" that would make sure the US avoided "playing catch-up" with the militaries of other nations.
At Tuesday's hearing, New York Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand accused the Trump administration of seeking "unlimited money for bombs" from Congress, while American citizens cannot afford to "feed their families".
She asked why Hegseth was asking for tens of billions of dollars for a war the president said had already been won.
The hearing culminated in a shouting match between Hegseth and Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
Peters called Hegseth a "failure" and said the Trump administration had created another "forever war".
Hegseth told Peters "shame on you", adding that the Michigan senator had "Trump derangement syndrome".
Most Democrats are opposed to the supplemental funding request, and there is discontent in Republican ranks too.
Some of the fiscal hawks in the Republican Party want spending cuts elsewhere to offset the budget.
Either way, the House of Representatives leaves town on Thursday and the two chambers of Congress will not be jointly back in session until September.
Even if Republicans can muster the votes, it's going to be a couple of months before the Pentagon can get the funds.
During Hegseth's hearing, Trump posted a list of longer, bloodier US wars, noting their duration and death toll.
He wrote on Truth Social that 18 had died so far in the US war with Iran, which began on 28 February.
On Tuesday, the Pentagon announced the death of Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton, a 30-year-old US soldier, in Iraq. It also said another US soldier Sgt Angel Rampersad, 28, was believed dead in Jordan.
A day earlier, the military identified two other US service personnel killed in action in Jordan as Pfc Isabella Gonzales, 19, and 1st Lt Tyler Feehan, 25.

sources.news_title: Hegseth says Iran war has cost US $37.5 BILLION as Senate debates funding
sources.text:
Hegseth says Iran war has cost US $37.5 billion as Senate debates funding
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing the U.S. war with Iran has cost $37.5 billion so far, as Republicans push a new $95 billion military funding packag
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has estimated that the costs of the war in Iran have reached $37.5 billion to date, as Republicans craft a $95 billion appropriations bill to support the military alongside additional White House initiatives.
Hegseth faced intense questioning and demonstrations on Tuesday over the U.S. conflict with Iran as he delivered an updated figure that was higher than previous estimates. At one point, he accused Democrats of suffering from "Trump Derangement Syndrome".
The contentious Senate Appropriations Committee session occurred days after the Pentagon revealed that three additional American service members had perished in the conflict, raising the fatalities to 17, with over 100 wounded since early July. His opening statement was disrupted multiple times by demonstrators.
- Hegseth slammed for 'disgusting' praise to Trump about dead US soldiers in Iran
- Hegseth reinstates 'patriots' after National Guard suspends 8 pilots for flyover
Hegseth characterized the supplemental war appropriations as an "urgent, necessary" capital infusion, and together with President Donald Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, a generational commitment to the armed forces.
"Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls," Hegseth testified. However, Sen. Patty Murray, the ranking Democrat on the committee, cautioned against "another forever war.
"This war is now spiraling out of control again," Murray said.
Iran War costs spiraling
President Donald Trump has repeatedly stated that "a deal is near, and the war will be over soon," she said. "But now, he's asking for $70 billion more - and for us to just trust him, it'll all work out fine."
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins also appeared before the committee. The proposed appropriations package includes $60 billion and $12 billion for additional national security needs, along with $10 billion for farm aid and $10 billion for voting law changes.
Prior to the hearing, the White House released a statement calling for support of the budget resolution "without modification - immediately."
War funding constitutes the bulk of the GOP's new budget proposal — a final priority package Republicans are eager to push through before lawmakers break for the midterm election campaign trail. The package is designed to support farmers struggling under Trump's tariffs and to finance changes to voter laws, with none of the spending offset by cuts elsewhere.
A majority of Americans continue to disapprove of Trump's handling of the Iran situation, according to an AP-NORC poll. Gas prices have surged as Iran moves to control oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. munitions are being depleted by the relentless American missile strikes, and Trump has distanced himself from his own campaign pledge to keep the U.S. out of prolonged military engagements.
Despite mounting pressure, Trump has shown no indication of stepping back from the conflict, and Republicans have largely declined to challenge his strategy or leverage Congress's budgetary and war powers authority to bring the fighting to a halt.
Ossoff demolishes Hegseth -- then Hegseth has an epic crashout
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) July 21, 2026
Sen. Jon Ossoff used Hegseth's premature declarations of victory against him during his Senate testimony, repeatedly reading back statements Hegseth made in March and April about Iran's military being "destroyed"… pic.twitter.com/KIFv6TW6Ir
Tough questions for Hegseth
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire challenged why Hegseth is requesting additional funding when the department has yet to allocate roughly half of the $150 billion Republicans allocated to the Pentagon in last year's major budget bill.
"Why are you asking the American people to absorb the cost of a war they don't support?" Shaheen asked.
As Hegseth began discussing the "historic nature" of Trump's military strategy, she interrupted him. Hegseth subsequently clarified that the remainder of last year's budget package would be allocated by September.
When GOP Sen. Mike Rounds inquired whether this funding request would be sufficient to "get the job done," the general hesitated.
"I can't answer the question on what it will cost, because the enemy has a vote," Caine said.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana was among several senators pressing for clarity on the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, questioning whether Iran will impose tolls on what has traditionally been an open waterway critical to oil transportation.
Caine responded: "That's a hypothetical question, and I don't know the answer to that."
Kennedy shot back: "Guys, we need straight answers."
Tensions intensified near the conclusion of the more than three-hour hearing. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., told Hegseth directly that his war claims don't add up.
Has the U.S. completely destroyed Iran's nuclear capabilities or not? she pressed.
"We're staying laser-focused on the objective," Hegseth responded, "and you're trying to make campaign commercials."
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. , questioned Hegseth on his previous assessments of the conflict, including the secretary's assertions regarding Iran's surrender.
When Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan characterized the administration's war strategy as an outright "failure," Hegseth fired back forcefully.
"Shame on you and others who call this a quagmire and a failure," Hegseth said.
Peters shot back at the secretary: "You, sir, are the failure."
The senator clarified that it is not U.S. troops who are falling short, but their commanders. "You don't have a strategy," Peters said.
"You don't have a long-term plan to actually win this war."
Hegseth accused Democrats of suffering from "Trump Derangement Syndrome" and alleged they were withholding necessary funding. Peters countered that the issue isn't financial, "but a question of leadership."

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth admits Iran conflict has cost US $37.5bn as he demands MORE cash to fund war effort
sources.text:
Pete Hegseth admits Iran conflict has cost US $37.5bn as he demands MORE cash to fund war effort
The Secretary of War has urged Congress to approve an additional $87billion in emergency Pentagon funding
Don't Miss
Most Read
Latest
The war with Iran has cost the United States an estimated $37.5billion (£28billion), according to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who has urged Congress to approve an additional $87billion (£65billion) in emergency Pentagon funding as the Middle East conflict continues.
Appearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee yesterday, Mr Hegseth said the conflict had become increasingly expensive, with costs climbing nearly $8billion (£6billion) since the Pentagon's last estimate in May.
Of the request for funding to near triple, $67billion (£50billion) would be allocated directly to military operations in the Middle East, while the remainder would support "broader defence priorities".
"We live in a dangerous world," Mr Hegseth told lawmakers, arguing the funding was essential to sustain military operations, replenish weapons and equipment, and ensure service members continued to receive pay.
He warned failure to approve the package would force cuts to military training and readiness at a time of heightened global tensions.
The hearing, Mr Hegseth's first appearance on Capitol Hill since fighting with the Islamic Republic resumed last week, was repeatedly interrupted by anti-war protesters and concluded with a heated exchange between the War Secretary and Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
Mr Peters accused the Trump administration of creating another "forever war", prompting Mr Hegseth to respond "shame on you" while accusing the senator of suffering from "Trump derangement syndrome".
The renewed conflict follows the collapse of a ceasefire agreed between Washington and Tehran in April.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has urged Congress to approve an additional $87billion in emergency Pentagon funding
| GETTYThe US has now carried out 11 consecutive days of strikes against Iranian targets, while Iran has responded with attacks on US forces and allies across the region.
Several American service members were confirmed killed in recent operations.
On Tuesday, officials announced the deaths of Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton in Iraq and Sgt Angel Rampersad in Jordan.
Earlier this week, the military also identified Pfc Isabella Gonzales and 1st Lt Tyler Feehan as having been killed in Jordan.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
President Donald Trump is expected to attend the dignified transfer of the fallen soldiers at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Wednesday.
While Mr Hegseth defended the funding request as a "generational investment" designed to maintain US military superiority, Democratic lawmakers questioned both the cost and the administration's strategy in light of the conflict's escalation.
Senator Patty Murray said the proposal "does not make a lot of sense", while Senator Kirsten Gillibrand accused the administration of seeking "unlimited money for bombs" while many Americans struggled with rising living costs.
Iran and the US have exchanged strikes throughout the month, despite brokering a deal to end the conflict
| US DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSEQuestions also emerged over whether the Pentagon's estimate fully reflects the financial burden of the conflict amid an impending attack on Pickaxe Mountain.
Sources familiar with the matter suggested the true cost could be significantly higher, arguing the published figure excludes expenses such as rebuilding damaged US military facilities.
Democrats remain largely opposed, while some Republican lawmakers are demanding spending cuts elsewhere to offset the additional defence costs.
With the House of Representatives set to recess this week and Congress not expected to reconvene fully until September, any vote on the emergency funding is likely to be delayed for several months.

sources.news_title: US Defense Secretary: Military operations against Iran cost $37.5 billion
sources.text:
Washington, July 22 (SANA)– US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed that the cost of US military operations against Iran has so far reached about $37.5 billion, an increase of nearly $8 billion over previously announced estimates.
Reuters quoted Hegseth as saying during a hearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee, in the presence of Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General Dan Keane: “This figure also includes extended and projected costs until the end of next September.”
These statements came during the U.S. Secretary of Defense’s first public appearance before lawmakers to answer questions regarding the financial costs and battlefield developments since Washington resumed its military operations in the region.
The region has been witnessing a rapidly escalating military confrontation since the U.S. military resumed strikes against Iranian targets and in the vicinity of the Strait of Hormuz, alongside growing international and economic warnings over the potential consequences of continued escalation for maritime security and global energy supplies.

sources.news_title: War in Iran has cost the US $37.5 billion so far, Pentagon says
sources.text:
War in Iran has cost the US $37.5 billion so far, Pentagon says
- Trump's administration estimated the first six days of the war had cost at least $11.3 billion
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth faced skeptical lawmakers to seek urgent funding for the unpopular Iran war, which has already cost $37.5 billion and risks further escalation.
- Rising financial cost of the Iran conflict.
- Lawmakers' skepticism and upcoming midterm elections.
- President Trump's threats of escalating targets.
- Impact on the Pentagon's budget and military readiness.
WASHINGTON: The cost of the United States’ war in Iran has risen to $37.5 billion so far, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday, as he faced skeptical lawmakers for the first time since heavy bombings resumed to seek urgent funding for the unpopular conflict.
With just six months before midterm elections in which President Donald Trump’s Republicans may face an uphill battle to keep their House of Representatives and Senate majorities, Democrats are riding high in public opinion polls as they attempt to link the unpopular Iran war with affordability.
Hegseth told lawmakers at a hearing in Washington that the $37.5 billion included certain aspects of the war as well as anticipated costs through September 30.
It was unclear how the Pentagon arrived at the figure. A source told Reuters in March that Trump’s administration estimated the first six days of the war had cost at least $11.3 billion.
US military says begins 11th straight night of strikes on Iran
Trump asked Congress last month for nearly $90 billion in additional funding, most of it related to the Iran conflict, setting the stage for another fight with lawmakers frustrated with the war and facing the November midterms.
Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have complained since the US and Israel began bombing Iran on February 28 that Trump and his team have not kept them informed about the conflict or his plans.
“The president is threatening escalation and war crimes, and suggesting this could be another forever war,” Senator Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said at the hearing.
Trump has repeatedly issued severe threats against Iran, including against civilian infrastructure, which critics say would be a war crime.
Trump’s Republicans hold such slim margins in the House and Senate that appropriations bills typically need Democratic support to pass.
“The reason why they (people) are so upset with you and this administration is because the words you have used in the past don’t add up,” Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said. “It’s either over, or it’s not over. It’s within two weeks, or it’s not two weeks, it’s either missiles or it’s not missiles.”
Impact of war
Hegseth also told lawmakers that military training would need to be curtailed without an urgent funding boost.
The war has strained the Pentagon’s nearly $1 trillion budget and risks funding for military personnel matters.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, acknowledged that potential cost during the hearing, saying that while they would figure out how to pay service members, the Pentagon could struggle with maintenance costs as well as investing in future capabilities.
Hegseth called on lawmakers to not just fund the supplemental request but also a $1.5 trillion budget request for 2027.
“Not funding this department at $1.5 trillion, I believe, is the greatest threat that our nation faces,” Hegseth said.
Hormuz vessel crossings fall further as security concerns linger
A fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran collapsed earlier this month and both sides have been carrying out daily strikes against each other.
The number of US troops killed in the war on Iran rose to 18 over the weekend, while roughly 430 US troops have been injured.
The Pentagon said on Monday that 100 service members were injured since July 7, but that 96% have returned to duty.
In the past week, Trump has threatened to expand the targets being struck in Iran to include energy plants and bridges, send ground forces to seize Iran’s Kharg Island oil hub and bomb a deep-underground nuclear-linked site known as Pickaxe Mountain.
On Tuesday, Trump said the US would take out the mountain facility “pretty soon.”

sources.news_title: Protests, heated exchanges mark Senate hearing as Hegseth says Iran war cost reached $37.5 billion
sources.text:
US War Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday (local time) revealed that the estimated cost of the war on Iran was around $37.5 billion so far. This comes as Republicans are preparing a package of $95 billion to fund the US military, besides other White House priorities.
Hegseth was answering at a combative Senate Appropriations Committee hearing where he provided the latest figure on the cost of the war.
His opening remarks at the hearing were disrupted a number of times by protestors.
The supplemental war funding is an “urgent, necessary” injection of money, Hegseth claimed, adding, “Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls.” Hegseth also said that this money will be used to “reinforce peace through strength.”
Senator Patty Murray, who was the top Democrat on the panel, warned of "another forever war.”
“This war is now spiraling out of control again,” Murray said.
The hearing came in the wake of three more US soldiers dying in the war against Iran and US President Donald Trump ordering fresh strikes on the country.
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins were also testifying before the panel. The proposed budget package includes $60 billion and $12 billion for other national security needs, along with $10 billion for farm aid and $10 billion for voting law changes.
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, a Democrat, asked Hegseth why the government wanted more money when they are yet to spend the $150 billion Republicans provided to Pentagon last year.
“Why are you asking the American people to absorb the cost of a war they don't support?” asked Shaheen.
She cut off Hegseth when he started describing the “historic nature” of Trump’s military strategy. The War Secretary later explained that the remainder of last year's budget package would be spent by September.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana was among several senators demanding answers over the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, asking if Iran will impose tolls on what historically has been an open waterway vital to the flow of oil.
Caine said, “That’s a hypothetical question, and I don’t know the answer to that.”
But Kennedy retorted: “Guys, we need straight answers.”
Tensions exploded toward the end of the more than three-hour hearing.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-NY, told Hegseth flatly that his war claims don't add up.
Has the US obliterated Iran's nuclear capabilities or not? she demanded to know.
“We're staying laser-focused on the objective,” Hegseth responded, “and you're trying to make campaign commercials.”
Sen Jon Ossoff, D-Ga, probed Hegseth's past assessments of the war, including the secretary's claims of Iran's surrender.
When Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan said the administration's war strategy has been a complete "failure," Hegseth erupted.
“Shame on you and others who call this a quagmire and a failure,” Hegseth said.
Peters told the secretary: “You, sir, are the failure."
The senator said it’s not the U.S. troops who are failing, but their leaders. “You don't have a strategy," Peters said. “You don't have a long-term plan to actually win this war.”
Hegseth said Democrats have “Trump Derangement Syndrome” and won't give him the money he needs.
Peters said it's not about money, “but a question of leadership.”
When Hegseth began his testimony with the words "we live in a dangerous world" and said that such a world requires bold and swift action, he was interrupted by protestors who shouted slogans against the US' war in Iran.
It was only after Chairwoman Collins banged her gavel and called for order that Hegseth was able to continue with his speech.
With AP inputs

sources.news_title: US War Secretary Hegseth Puts Cost of Iran War at USD 37.5 Billion So Far
sources.text:
World News | US War Secretary Hegseth Puts Cost of Iran War at USD 37.5 Billion So Far
Get latest articles and stories on World at LatestLY. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Tuesday (local time) estimated that the cost of the ongoing US conflict with Iran has reached USD 37.5 billion so far, including certain operations and maintenance expenses projected through the end of the current fiscal year.
Washington DC [US], July 22 (ANI): US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Tuesday (local time) estimated that the cost of the ongoing US conflict with Iran has reached USD 37.5 billion so far, including certain operations and maintenance expenses projected through the end of the current fiscal year.
Hegseth disclosed the figure during a hearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee while responding to questions from Democratic Senator Dick Durbin.

"The estimate we have as of today is USD 37.5 billion," Hegseth said, adding that the amount included "certain aspects of it" as well as some anticipated military operations and maintenance costs through September 30.
The estimate marks the latest official assessment of the financial impact of the conflict and is around USD 8 billion higher than the USD 29 billion figure previously cited by the Trump administration in May.

In May, Jay Hurst, a senior Pentagon official who is performing the duties of Pentagon Comptroller, informed a House Appropriations Committee hearing that the US military campaign against the Islamic Republic had cost nearly USD 29 billion, revising upward the earlier estimate of USD 25 provided to the US Congress two weeks ago.

sources.news_title: On Iran, a $37 billion price tag and no answers on how it ends
sources.text:
“We need some hard answers and some straight talk.”
Republican Sen. John Kennedy dispensed with his usual folksy patter to speak bluntly for the nation Tuesday on Capitol Hill.
Kennedy and Americans who want to know how long President Donald Trump’s war will last and at what cost were looking for answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
They didn’t get them.
Instead, most Republicans stood firm in a critical hearing with an administration waging a hugely unpopular war, while Democrats highlighted the gap between its premature victory laps and the current stalemate.
In the hearing’s most illuminating moment, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff told Hegseth: “You will not answer whether your statement made on the 14th day of the war that Iran’s military had been quote destroyed and made combat ineffective was a truthful statement to the American people as you sit here and ask for tens of billions (of dollars) more.”
The Georgia senator’s monotone but relentless cross-examination extracted the hearing’s critical takeaway: The administration is asking for a huge windfall in financing for a war it has always struggled to explain, can’t control and for which it lacks metrics of success and a way out.
Hegseth, and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, came armed with an $87.6 billion Trump administration supplemental request that includes more than $67 billion for the war and other Pentagon spending.
And as Hegseth announced that the conflict had racked up $37.5 billion in costs, it is expanding. More US troops died over the weekend, bringing the death toll to 18; CNN reported that 100 American personnel had been injured since early July; Iran has all but closed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz; its Houthi allies in Yemen are threatening alternative Red Sea routes; and Trump warned Tuesday he would “soon” order another escalation, with an attack on Pickaxe Mountain, another suspected Iranian nuclear site.
A daunting new reality
Hegseth and Caine mostly dodged. And it was a masterstroke for the White House to send Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, a talented politician, to testify on a supplemental that seeks $11 billion for producers affected by winter storms. After all, every senator has a farm problem.
But as Hegseth praised Trump for launching the war and blamed the Biden administration for everything, and Caine gingerly piloted himself away from partisan storms, the hearing did end up shedding a little more light than the administration may have hoped.
It’s now clear that failure of the Memorandum of Understanding that briefly stopped the fighting has narrowed the administration’s war aims and — many Americans will not be pleased to hear — left them apparently more open ended.
            Once, Trump spoke of regime change in Iran, of unleashing its people to reclaim their country and of transforming the Middle East. But Hegseth, pressed repeatedly on what victory looks like, was vague. “You asked me what the overarching objective is, and I would say ensuring Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said. He later added : “Ultimately, a lot of the strikes … are taking Iran’s ability to see and sense away in the Strait of Hormuz.”
    
This will be concerning news for Americans wary of Middle East entanglements for two specific reasons.
First, the administration said last year it had “obliterated” Iran’s capacity to ever build a nuclear weapon with its strikes on atomic plants. If that was true, why did Trump launch the war this year? If it wasn’t, it suggests the US will have to perpetually be ready to use military action to tamp down Iranian nuclear activity.
Second, Hegseth’s comments also seem to point to prolonged US military action. After all, the Strait was open when the war began. And even if the current US bombardment works, it might require constant vigilance and attacks to halt missile and drone strikes on oil and gas tankers.
Some of Trump’s comments Tuesday also supported the idea that the war could drag on. He told reporters in the Oval Office that the midterm elections in November wouldn’t impact his strategy. “I don’t view it as ‘Gee we’re having an election in a period of time,’” he said. This will be bad news for Republican candidates amid a war that polls show a majority of Americans oppose.
And later in the day, Trump seemed to imply that a longer war in Iran wouldn’t be a big deal, in historical terms. He compared the 18 US combat deaths in the Iran war with losses in other modern military engagements, including the 58,000 killed in Vietnam and death tolls in the low thousands in Iraq and Afghanistan.
His post struck some critics as disrespectful to the fallen. Trump will attend a dignified transfer service Wednesday at Dover Air Force Base for the remains of soldiers lost over the weekend.
The President often changes his mind on a dime — so nothing is ever certain. A sudden reversal might even be likely if gas prices zoom up, global oil reserves wane and economic costs again stir damaging political winds.
But the administration — unlike at the start of the war — is not setting timelines measured in weeks for the war to be over and troops to come home.
Democrats test their 2026 voter appeal
The hearing also tested the Democratic Party’s emerging midterm message. The linkage between a deeply unpopular war and the affordability crisis facing millions of Americans was best expressed by New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand.
“Secretary Hegseth, you’re requesting billions of dollars in supplemental funding for a war that you said would last for weeks and that the president has no plan or ability to end,” Gillibrand told Hegseth. “(Voters) have seen their grocery and gas bills rise, and this unpopular and unauthorized war abroad is a higher priority to this administration than their ability to feed their families and provide healthcare to their loved ones who are sick.”
Hegseth argued that politics was about trade-offs and preventing a nuclear Iran was a long-run cost saving measure. He had a point, in both geopolitical and financial terms. But justifying real time economic pain by citing a distant threat is hardly likely to help GOP candidates.
Despite the vague and sometimes disconcerting administration messaging, most Republicans in the room stood firm beside Hegseth and backed the supplemental.
The session didn’t deteriorate into the performative shout fest that most congressional hearings become in a poisoned political age — at least until the final questions, when Michigan Sen. Gary Peters blasted Hegseth as a “failure” and the Defense Secretary slammed what he called Democratic “cowardice.”
Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins set a courteous and respectful tone. But Collins, the most endangered Republican senator in the midterms, would hardly have welcomed signs the war is far from over.
And a perception that the administration may not be talking about an exit strategy — because there isn’t one — could create political repercussions that go far beyond her seat in Maine, which could decide who runs the Senate next year.

sources.news_title: 'Urgent requirements’ for US military funding cited by GOP as Hegseth estimates war cost • Maine Morning Star
sources.text:
‘Urgent requirements’ for US military funding cited by GOP as Hegseth estimates war cost
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate committee in charge of funding the government spent hours in a hearing room Tuesday, trying to parse out just how much extra spending lawmakers should provide for the military amid the ongoing war in Iran.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators the bombing of Iran has cost $37.5 billion. He said that while the department has about $75 billion in unobligated funds from Republicans’ “big, beautiful” law, that money wasn’t intended to cover the costs of the war.
Republicans and Democrats on the Appropriations Committee also heard from three of their colleagues about the need for natural disaster recovery funding and the secretary of Agriculture about her request for emergency aid for farmers.
Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, summed up the multitude of proposals for additional money by saying the “country has many urgent funding needs.”
Collins said that while there were vastly different views among senators on the panel about the war, “the fact remains that there are must-pay bills and urgent requirements facing the department that affect the ability of our troops to be well trained and more broadly of the U.S. military to deter and defend against potential aggressors worldwide.”
Washington Democratic Sen. Patty Murray, ranking member on the committee, said at the beginning of the three-and-a-half hour hearing the United States “is no safer or better off than before the war.”
“In fact, we are considerably less safe. Our stockpiles have been depleted and it will take years of production to fully replenish them no matter how much money is thrown at this problem,” Murray said.
By the end of the hearing, she indicated Democrats may not support any emergency funding for the Defense Department related to the Iran war.
“Unfortunately, this hearing has done exceptionally little to justify the president’s request or to instill confidence that this administration has an exit plan or a strategy to end the war,” Murray said. “This war has cost us a lot. The last thing we should be doing is rubber stamping another $70 billion to help Trump keep it going.”
Hegseth warns of ‘critical shortfalls’
Hegseth said that without extra money from Congress, the department would “face critical shortfalls that threaten” its ability to “pay our service members, rapidly replenish equipment and munitions, and sustain vital operations without disruption.”
Hegseth repeatedly defended the Iran war during the hearing, pressing back on criticism from several Democrats that it was similar to earlier wars in the Middle East.
“President Trump said we’re not fighting stupid wars like that again and he hasn’t,” Hegseth said. “That’s why we haven’t been trying to remake Iranian society, but simply in the realist America First way, ensure they never have a path to a nuclear bomb, full stop.”
He declined to go into detail in a non-classified setting about the aid China and Russia has provided to Iran, but did say those two countries are “enabling some of the things Iran is doing.”
Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. John D. Caine said he’d prefer not discuss the intelligence about those two countries.
“I’d rather not opine on the specifics because that would divulge what we know. And I never want the adversary to know what I know. I just want to know it,” he said.
Caine also declined to go into any level of detail about whether the administration has contemplated sending ground troops into Iran.
“I think it’d be unhelpful for me to opine on hypothetical situations on whatever decisions the president may or may not take in the future,” Caine said.
Trump request to Congress
Congress approved $838.7 billion for the Defense Department in February as part of the annual government funding process. A few weeks later, President Donald Trump began bombing Iran, starting a war that has led to the deaths of 17 U.S. service members — including three in the last few days — and injured more than 445.
The administration sent a supplemental spending request to Congress in late June, asking lawmakers to provide $87.6 billion in emergency funding. It proposed an additional:
- $67.15 billion for the Defense Department
- $11.1 billion for the Agriculture Department to provide aid to farmers
- $3.36 billion for the State Department for diplomatic, security and global health programs
- $2.03 billion for the U.S. Coast Guard
- $1 billion for the Transportation Department to “to assist in the final design and construction of a modernized Penn Station in New York City”
- $1 billion for the Labor Department to “increase the benefit levels for participants of certain pension plans that were sponsored by Delphi Corporation and terminated as a result of General Motors’ bankruptcy in 2009″
- $767.5 million for the Energy Department
- $600 million for the General Services Administration’s federal buildings fund
- $500 million for the National Park Service to upgrade a seawall and improve the World War II Memorial
- $40.26 million for the FBI for its role in the Iran war and “other classified needs”
- $36.18 million for the Treasury Department’s office of terrorism and financial intelligence
- $13.1 million for the Homeland Security Department’s operations and support account that was part of a “classified request.”
House Republicans want to use the complex budget reconciliation process to provide up to $60 billion for the Defense Department and $12 billion for farm aid.
But that effort hasn’t yet garnered the support from Senate Republicans needed to advance. GOP lawmakers used the same process last year to bolster defense funding by about $150 billion in the “big, beautiful” law.
That means the most likely path to provide extra money for the war and farmers will be a bipartisan supplemental spending bill, likely written by the Appropriations Committees.
With the House set to leave Thursday for its August recess and the Senate planning to leave for its break on Aug. 6, the earliest any additional funding would become law is September.
Farm aid
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the administration’s request for emergency funding would help farmers, including those who have experienced extreme weather events.
Collins, however, questioned the administration’s decision to limit its request for supplemental funding to agriculture losses that took place during the last year.
“Many of our producers are struggling amid a combination of market volatility and disaster conditions last year, which included excessive rainfall in the spring, followed by a severe drought. They need relief. Yet the administration’s supplemental request does not include funding to address these recovery needs,” Collins said. “It does have $1.1 billion to help Florida agricultural producers rebound from a severe freeze this past winter. But nothing for prior disasters in other states.”
Rollins said she would be in full support of Congress providing more funding than requested for farmers affected by severe weather events.
Oregon Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley asked Rollins to ensure the Office of Management and Budget sends lawmakers a specific request to address ongoing costs related to wildfires.
“Senators are asking for a number from OMB in order to go forward,” he said. “And when we’re looking at the fires right now, my home state is in the epicenter of the highest risk in the country.”
Rollins said she would “absolutely” get that number to lawmakers, adding it “is a paramount importance, especially in the middle of fire season right now.”

The Pentagon has raised its official estimate for the cost of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran to $37.5 billion, as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended a broader request for nearly $70 billion in supplemental war funding during a Senate hearing.
Pentagon Raises Official Iran War Cost To $37.5 Billion
On Tuesday, appearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hegseth said the war has cost an estimated $37.5 billion so far, marking an $8.5 billion increase from the Trump administration’s previous estimate of $29 billion released in May, Al Jazeera reported.
“The estimate we have as of today is $37.5 billion,” Hegseth told lawmakers, adding that the figure includes certain operations and maintenance costs through the end of September, though he did not provide a detailed breakdown.
The updated estimate comes as the Pentagon seeks nearly $70 billion in supplemental funding tied to the Iran conflict as part of President Donald Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget.
Calling the funding request essential, Hegseth told senators, “Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” describing the supplemental package as an “urgent, necessary” investment in national defense, noted Fortune.
Democrats Challenge Pentagon’s Spending Request
The hearing grew contentious as Democratic lawmakers questioned both the rising cost of the conflict and the administration’s broader defense spending priorities.
Sen. Patty Murray criticized the expansive budget proposal, noting that it also includes funding for National Guard deployments in Washington, D.C., border security operations and military missions targeting alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean.
“So I’ll be blunt,” Murray said. “The truth is, your request does not make a lot of sense.”
The hearing was interrupted multiple times by protesters, days after the Pentagon announced that three additional U.S. service members had died in the conflict, bringing the total American death toll to 17, while more than 100 troops have been injured since early July.
Political Divide Deepens Over Iran War
Senate Republicans defended the defense package on X, arguing it would boost military pay, improve housing and expand recruiting, while accusing Senate Democrats of blocking the legislation.
Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) wrote on X that the hearing confirmed the Iran conflict is “a war in search of a mission,” adding, “This war must end, NOW.”
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) also criticized the administration on X, saying Americans are “paying the price for Trump’s war as costs continue to rise,” while questioning whether the growing military expenditures are making the country safer.

sources.news_title: Hegseth: Iran War Cost Now at $37.5 Billion
sources.text:
The Pentagon’s cost estimate for the Iran war has risen to $37.5 billion, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a congressional committee July 21—and without emergency supplemental funding, the military will have to “curtail” training to cover those costs, he added.
Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine appeared before the Senate Appropriations Committee to defend the White House’s supplemental funding request from last month, which includes $67.1 billion in defense spending. But the wide-ranging hearing reinforced how complex the Pentagon’s overall budget outlook has become, especially with the cost of the Iran conflict expected to keep rising as hostilities reintensify.
Even the new cost estimate is not completely straightforward. Hegseth told Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) that the total includes some military pay, operations and maintenance, and “other anticipated costs” through the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, but it apparently does not include any costs to repair or rebuild military infrastructure damaged in the conflict.
Regardless of how the estimate is calculated, those costs carry an impact, Hegseth told Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).
“There is training, training right now and training in the future, that would have to be curtailed if we do not get our budget needs met and met urgently,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth’s comments appear to confirm a report from The Washington Post that some military training and exercises have been canceled or delayed to divert funds for Iran operations.
Back in late April, the Pentagon’s acting comptroller Jules “Jay” Hurst III estimated the cost of the conflict to be $25 billion, though he cautioned the total was not completely comprehensive and did not include military construction costs. Hurst revised that estimate to $29 billion by early May, and White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought said in late June that the cost was up to $30 billion.
In the last 10 days, U.S. Central Command has launched a series of large-scale strikes in retaliation for Iranian strikes on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, as the fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed. That’s led the U.S. Air Force to rush fighter jets to the region. All these moves carry financial costs.
Supplemental Squeeze
The full supplemental funding request the White House sent Congress on June 24 includes $87.6 billion. The bulk of that—$67.1 billion—is for the Pentagon, but exactly how much of that is meant to pay for the Iran conflict is less clear, defense budget analysts have previously noted to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
In a letter to Congress, OMB said the request included $21 billion for munitions, $17.3 billion for operational costs, and $1.5 billion for fuel costs, all of which could be counted as related to Iran. But other elements, like $4 billion for high-priority Space Force programs, $5.1 billion for cybersecurity and autonomy, and $1.7 billion for drones, were unrelated.
“The president’s request is not even primarily a request to cover the costs of the Iran war,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) argued. “This request is chock full of asks to fund unrelated DOD priorities, which should be considered through our annual appropriations process, not in an emergency supplemental.”
In written testimony, Hegseth broke down the request between $21.3 billion for “sustaining military readiness” and $45.9 billion for “accelerating critical capabilities.” While never explicitly mentioning Iran operations in the statement, Hegseth did categorize $15.1 billion of the request as being “for core operational costs, funding military pay, and operational shortfalls in training and readiness accounts and other mission-related costs” and $2 billion to “replace equipment lost or damaged during combat operations.” The $21 billion in munitions would go toward “high-demand” weapons like Joint Direct Attack Munitions, hypersonics, and more.
In her own statement, Collins argued that the supplemental is critical to making sure service members have what they need.
“We should not undermine the readiness of our service members for any engagement or refuse to rebuild critical capabilities,” Collins said. “Our men and women in uniform do not decide where they are sent or the missions to which they are assigned. Congress has a responsibility to ensure that they have the tools, the training, and the support that they need to accomplish their missions.”
Many Democrats on the committee, though, signaled they view supporting the supplemental as supporting the Trump administration’s approach to the Iran conflict.
It appears congressional Republicans are preparing to forge ahead with the supplemental without any Democratic support—over in the House, Republicans are in the midst of advancing a budget resolution with $60 billion for defense through the reconciliation process, a maneuver designed to circumvent the Senate’s requirement for a supermajority of 60 votes to pass.
While the White House and congressional Republicans had previously talked about including $350 billion from the Pentagon’s 2027 budget request in this reconciliation bill—the third Congress is pursuing in this session—now leaders are saying the legislation’s $60 billion will go toward Iran war costs and munitions, the priorities identified in the supplemental.
